Legume Spring Summer

Medicago sativa

A planted hay legume, not a common wild plant, but ordinary on New England farms and in hay.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    House Rabbit Society treats alfalfa hay as suitable for growing rabbits and a limited hay for adults because of the calcium.

    Fresh alfalfa is gassier than hay. Introduce it slowly.

  • Chicken Limit

    Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

  • Duck Limit Uncertain

    Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A duck-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Goose Limit Uncertain

    Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A goose-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Turkey Limit Uncertain

    Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A turkey-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A quail-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Guinea pig Limit

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

  • Goat Limit

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

  • Sheep Limit

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

  • Pig Limit

    Alfalfa is rich feed. Lush stands cause frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Adult rabbits get more calcium than they need from a diet of alfalfa hay.

    Dried hay is appropriate for growing rabbits. For adult rabbits, timothy or orchardgrass should be the usual hay. Ruminants should not get a sudden meal of wet alfalfa.

  • Cattle Limit

    Alfalfa is a standard dairy forage and a classic cause of frothy bloat when it is lush.

    Wilt a fresh cutting. Do not turn hungry cattle onto a pure wet stand.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Three leaflets, the center one on a short stalk, and purple flower clusters. The seed pods spiral.

Lookalikes

Black medic is a low relative with yellow flowers and black pods. Clovers lack the stalked center leaflet.

Parts to feed

Leaves and fine stems. Mature stems are woody.

New England timing

First cut is often late May or June in southern New England, later north. Later cuts follow through the summer if the stand is irrigated or the season is wet.

Harvest

Cut at bud or early flower for the best feed. Lush wet alfalfa is a bloat risk for ruminants.

Preparation

Dried alfalfa hay is the usual form for rabbits. Wilt fresh cuttings before ruminants get them. Do not feed moldy hay.

Legume Summer

Trifolium hybridum

A clover with a poor reputation because of liver and photosensitivity disease, best documented in horses.

Uncertain: Disease reports are strongest for horses, which this guide does not cover. The limit for the other species is a caution, not a count of cases.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit Uncertain

    Alsike clover is linked to photosensitivity and liver disease, with the clearest reports in horses. Other stock should not get it as a chosen forage.

    A trace in mixed hay is a different situation from a bundle of alsike. Do not harvest it on purpose.

  • Chicken Limit Uncertain

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Upright, hairless, with a flower head that is white and pink on the same plant. Leaflets lack the white crescent of white clover.

Lookalikes

White clover creeps and the flower stalk is leafless. Red clover is hairy.

Parts to feed

Not a chosen feed. If it is mixed into hay, it should not dominate the bale.

New England timing

Flowers in midsummer. It shows up in New England hay mixes and on damp ground.

Harvest

Do not cut a pure stand to feed.

Preparation

Drying does not make a heavy alsike cutting a good feed.

Toxic parts: Cornell lists leaves, twigs, roots and unripe fruit. Colorado State says all parts are poisonous, especially when wilted. We show the Cornell list.

  • Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock: Sambucus canadensis (Elderberry)
    Sambucus canadensis. Species most often affected: cattle, humans, goats. Poisonous parts: leaves, twigs, roots, unripe fruits. Primary poisons: sambunigrin.
  • NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox: Sambucus canadensis (American Elder, American Elderberry, Common Elderberry, Elderberry)
    Poisonous to humans. Poison severity: Low. Poison part: Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Stems. Toxic principle: Cyanogenic glycoside and alkaloid.
  • Colorado State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Guide to Poisonous Plants: Elderberry (Sambucus L.)
    Animals affected: Cattle, sheep Toxic principle: Cyanogenic glycoside sambunigrin which is hydrolysed in the rumen by microorganisms to free hydrogen cyanide (HCN). All parts of the plant are poisonous especially if wilted or in regrowth. The Cyanide blocks the action of cytochrome oxidase that prevents hemoglobin fro…

Identification

A shrub with opposite compound leaves, white flat flower clusters, and dark berries. Twigs have a white pith.

Lookalikes

Pokeweed is an herb with alternate leaves and a red stem, and it is also toxic. Water hemlock is an herb, not a shrub, and is deadly.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, bark, or unripe berries.

New England timing

It flowers white in June and July in New England wet edges. Purple-black fruit follows. Leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are the cyanide problem.

Harvest

Do not strip leafy stems for a basket.

Preparation

Do not dry the leaves for feed.

A common New England yard and orchard tree. Fresh twigs are a rabbit chew. Wilted leaves are a cyanide risk.

Who can eat it

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Simple oval leaves with a fine tooth, and a fruit that is clearly an apple. Crabapples count as this entry.

Lookalikes

Cherry leaves are similar and smell like bitter almond when crushed. Cherry is a separate, stricter entry. If you are not sure it is apple, do not feed the leaves.

Parts to feed

Fresh twigs in moderation. Not wilted leaves. Not seeds. Fruit flesh only as a small treat.

New England timing

Twigs can be cut in winter and early spring. Leaves are on the tree from May to October. Wilted leaves after a storm or a pruning pile are the dangerous form. Fruit drops in September and October.

Harvest

Offer prunings fresh, the same day, or not at all. Do not feed a pile of leaves that sat and wilted.

Preparation

Do not dry apple leaves for feed. Remove seeds if you offer fruit. A whole apple is a lot of sugar for a rabbit.

Identification

Five leaflets (three at the tip, two at the base) and yellow pea flowers. The pods spread like a bird's foot.

Lookalikes

Crown vetch has pink flowers and climbs. Yellow sweet clover is much taller, with tiny flowers along the stem.

Parts to feed

Leafy tops.

New England timing

Flowers and pods in July and August. It is planted in New England pastures and also escapes.

Harvest

Cut in flower or just before. It is a pasture plant more than a bulk hay plant.

Preparation

Fresh or dried, as part of a mix. It contains tannins, which is why bloat is less common, and those tannins are a reason not to overdo it.

Identification

Purple flowers with yellow centers and bright red egg-shaped berries. Leaves are often lobed at the base.

Lookalikes

Oriental bittersweet is a woody twiner with orange capsules that split to show red seeds. That vine is not this plant, and it is not a feed either.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or berries.

New England timing

It vines through New England hedges and flowers and fruits from midsummer into fall.

Harvest

Do not strip it off a fence for animals.

Preparation

Cooking is not a step in this guide. Leave the plant.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Alternate simple leaves, fine teeth, and a scratch on the twig that smells like bitter almond. Mature bark looks like burnt cornflakes. White flower spikes, then dark fruit.

Lookalikes

Apple leaves do not smell of bitter almond. If a crushed leaf or scratched twig smells like almond, treat it as cherry and do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or wilted twigs. Fruit is not the forage product.

New England timing

Leaves are dangerous whenever they wilt, which in New England includes summer storm damage and the fall of leaves. Pin cherry and chokecherry deserve the same refusal.

Harvest

Do not throw prunings over the fence.

Preparation

Wilting increases the danger. Do not dry the leaves for feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Compound leaves, a pair of short thorns at the nodes, and hanging clusters of white pea flowers. The pods are flat.

Lookalikes

Honey locust has much larger branched thorns and long twisted pods. Do not feed either on the strength of the other.

Parts to feed

Do not feed bark, seeds, leaves, or sprouts.

New England timing

It flowers white in late May and June along New England fences and roads. Bark, sprouts, and seeds are the worst parts.

Harvest

Do not toss locust prunings into a pen.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Browse Spring Summer Fall

Rubus allegheniensis · bramble, black raspberry leaves are used the same way

A bramble. Leaves are a standard rabbit green and goat browse. Other Rubus species in the region, including black raspberry, are used the same way.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Safe

    Watch for poison ivy growing through the patch. Do not grab canes bare-handed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Arching canes with thorns, leaves usually in fives, and white flowers followed by black aggregate fruit that does not slip off a core.

Lookalikes

Multiflora rose has a different flower and a hip, not a blackberry. Poison ivy can thread through a bramble patch and has three glossy leaflets and no thorns.

Parts to feed

Leaves and young cane tips. Fruit is fine for poultry and pigs in season. Thorns are the practical limit for the person cutting it and for wool.

New England timing

Leaves are useful from May until frost. Fruit ripens in late July and August in much of New England, later in the north.

Harvest

Clip leafy tips with gloves. Leave the old woody cane.

Preparation

Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting is required for safety.

Sources

Forb Toxic to some animals Spring Summer Fall

Pteridium aquilinum

A native fern that causes a serious poisoning, including bone-marrow failure and tumors in cattle, and thiamine deficiency in horses.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Bracken contains ptaquiloside and a thiaminase. Cattle develop bone-marrow failure and urinary tumors. Other stock should not be fed it either. Sheep tolerate more before they show signs, which is not the same as a safe feed.

    Do not cut it for any animal in this guide.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A single coarse triangular frond, divided, often waist-high, rising separately from a underground rhizome rather than in a crown.

Lookalikes

Ostrich fern grows in a crown in floodplains and is not a livestock feed either. If you cannot name the fern, do not feed it. This guide does not treat other ferns as forage.

Parts to feed

Do not feed fronds, fresh or dried.

New England timing

Fiddleheads appear in May. Fronds are toxic through the summer and in dried hay. It is common on New England dry slopes and old fields.

Harvest

Keep bracken out of hay cuttings.

Preparation

Drying does not remove the toxin. There is no safe amount to aim for.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Shiny yellow flowers with five petals and divided leaves. Several species grow in New England. All fresh buttercups get the same caution.

Lookalikes

Cinquefoil has strawberry-like leaves and is not this plant. Lesser celandine grows low and wet in early spring and is also not a feed.

Parts to feed

Do not feed fresh plants.

New England timing

Flowers from May into July in New England hay meadows. The fresh plant is the problem. Fully dried hay loses most of the irritant.

Harvest

Do not add buttercup to a fresh bundle.

Preparation

This guide is about fresh harvest. Do not cut buttercup for fresh feed. Hay that is fully dry is a different product, and a bale that is mostly buttercup is still poor feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Feathery leaves from a known garden row or from carrots you bought.

Lookalikes

Poison hemlock leaves are finer and the plant is hairless with a spotted stem. Do not go to a roadside to cut carrot tops.

Parts to feed

Leaves of garden carrots. Roots are a treat, not forage.

New England timing

Garden carrot tops are available from July until the roots are dug, often into October.

Harvest

Cut tops from your row or use tops from carrots you bought. Wash them.

Preparation

Feed fresh. A large amount from heavily fertilized ground is unnecessary because of nitrate.

Who can eat it

Identification

Large hairy leaves, the upper ones running down the stem, and clusters of nodding pink, purple, or white bells.

Lookalikes

Foxglove has smoother leaves and thimble flowers on a tall spike, and is also toxic. Do not guess between them.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves.

New England timing

Garden plants leaf out in May and flower through the summer. It is planted in New England gardens and persists for years.

Harvest

Do not cut it for animals.

Preparation

Drying does not remove pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A low mat, opposite leaves, and a line of hairs on one side of the stem. Small white flowers with five petals so deeply split they look like ten.

Lookalikes

Scarlet pimpernel, which is not a feed here, has orange or blue flowers and no hair line on the stem. Mouse-ear chickweed is hairier.

Parts to feed

Tender tops.

New England timing

Best in April, May, and again in September and October. It can linger in a mild early winter in southern New England. Summer plants are stringy.

Harvest

Cut the tops. Do not take a mat full of soil.

Preparation

Feed fresh, in a mix. Very large amounts are unnecessary. It wilts fast, which is fine.

Sources

Asclepias syriaca

A native milkweed. The latex is poisonous. It is not forage, even though insects eat it.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Common milkweed contains cardiac glycosides and other toxins. Livestock are poisoned by the leaves and stems.

    Do not feed it because monarch caterpillars eat it. That says nothing about a goat or a rabbit.

Identification

Opposite, thick, oval leaves, a stout stem, milky sap, and round clusters of dusty-pink flowers. Pods are warty.

Lookalikes

Dogbane also has milky sap and is poisonous. Spreading dogbane is branched with smaller pods. Either plant stays out of the basket.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, pods, or flowers.

New England timing

It is in full leaf from June through August along New England fields and roads.

Harvest

Do not cut it for feed.

Preparation

Drying does not make milkweed a safe green.

Forb Toxic to some animals Summer

Hypericum perforatum

A roadside weed that causes sunburn in light-skinned stock.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Hypericin in St. John's wort causes photosensitization: unpigmented skin blisters in the sun. Cattle, sheep, and goats are the usual cases.

    Do not feed it, and do not turn light-skinned animals onto a stand of it.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Yellow flowers with five petals and many stamens. Hold a leaf to the light: it looks perforated with tiny clear dots.

Lookalikes

Other yellow weeds lack those translucent dots. If you do not see them, you are not looking at this plant, and an unnamed yellow weed is still not automatically safe.

Parts to feed

Do not feed tops or hay made from a heavy stand.

New England timing

It flowers along New England roads in July. The photosensitizing pigment is in the fresh plant and in hay.

Harvest

Leave it out of the cutting.

Preparation

Drying does not remove hypericin.

Digitaria sanguinalis · hairy crabgrass

A weedy grass that livestock and poultry take readily.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Stems that root at the nodes and spread like a crab. Finger-like seed heads.

Lookalikes

Foxtail has a bristly cylindrical head. Those bristles can injure mouths, so do not substitute foxtail for this plant.

Parts to feed

Leaves and tender stems. Skip bristly seed heads of any grass mixed in.

New England timing

A summer annual. In New England it is useful from July until frost, especially in gardens and beaten ground.

Harvest

Pull or cut the leafy growth. Shake out soil.

Preparation

Feed fresh the same day. Piles of crabgrass heat quickly.

Identification

Sprawling stems, compound leaves, and a circle of pink-and-white pea flowers. Seed pods are slender.

Lookalikes

Birdsfoot trefoil has yellow flowers. Hairy vetch has purple flowers and obviously hairy stems.

Parts to feed

Do not feed any part.

New England timing

It flowers along New England roads from June into August. It was planted for erosion control and escaped.

Harvest

Keep it out of the basket.

Preparation

There is no preparation that makes it a feed.

Forb Spring Summer

Rumex crispus · sheep sorrel is the same oxalate caution

A common New England weed. Oxalate is the reason to limit it. Sheep sorrel is a smaller relative with the same caution.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Dock and sorrel are oxalate plants. Small amounts are tolerated. A diet of them is not.

    Keep dock as a minor part of a mix. Do not feed it to an animal that already gets other high-oxalate greens the same day.

Identification

Long leaves with wavy margins in a rosette, and a tall stalk of green flowers that turns rusty brown.

Lookalikes

Burdock has huge heart-shaped leaves that are not wavy in the same way. Skunk cabbage grows in wet muck and smells skunky when torn.

Parts to feed

Young leaves, sparingly. Not the seed stalk.

New England timing

Basal leaves are best in May and June. The rusty seed stalks stand through fall and are not the feed.

Harvest

Take a few leaves from a plant, not the whole stand.

Preparation

Feed fresh and limited. Drying does not remove oxalate.

Identification

Strap leaves and a yellow or white flower with a trumpet, from a bulb.

Lookalikes

Iris has a flat fan of leaves and a different flower, and it is not given a safe verdict here either. If it is a spring bulb, do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or bulbs.

New England timing

Leaves come up in April and May across New England yards. Bulbs are in the ground all year and are the most dangerous part.

Harvest

Do not toss divided bulbs to pigs or poultry.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A basal rosette of toothed leaves, hollow flower stalks, and a single yellow head. The plant has milky sap.

Lookalikes

Catsear has branched, solid stalks and hairy leaves. Hawkweeds are hairy. Those are not substitutes without their own identification.

Parts to feed

Leaves and flowers. Roots are not needed for feed.

New England timing

The best leaves are April through early June, then again in September and October. Midsummer leaves are bitter. Flowers follow the spring leaves.

Harvest

Cut leaves from unsprayed ground. Wash grit off. Skip plants from a chemically treated lawn.

Preparation

Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting is required for safety. Large wet amounts can loosen stools.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Broad, pleated leaves that clasp a stout stem, in wet soil. The flower cluster is a branching green-yellow spike.

Lookalikes

Skunk cabbage has leaves that come from the ground, not up a tall stem, and it smells skunky. Both are toxic. Indian poke is another name for false hellebore, not for a table vegetable.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or roots.

New England timing

It stands in wet New England meadows and streambanks from May into July. All of the above-ground growth is dangerous.

Harvest

Do not cut it.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Identification

A tall spike of spotted thimble flowers and a rosette of soft, broad leaves.

Lookalikes

Comfrey has bell flowers that nod in a cluster, not a tall one-sided spike of thimbles. Both are toxic.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or flowers.

New England timing

It flowers in June and July in New England gardens and sometimes escapes. Leaves are toxic before the flower opens.

Harvest

Do not cut the flower spike for any animal.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairless vine you planted, with tendrils, white flowers, and pea pods.

Lookalikes

Sweet pea is an ornamental with different flowers and poisonous seeds. Hairy vetch is hairy and purple-flowered and is toxic. If you did not plant it, do not treat it as a garden pea.

Parts to feed

Vines, leaves, and pods of garden pea.

New England timing

Vines are available as the pods fill, often June and July, and again in a fall planting in warmer parts of the region.

Harvest

Cut spent vines from the garden row.

Preparation

Feed fresh. Do not feed moldy vines.

Forb Spring

Alliaria petiolata

An invasive mustard. It is not a studied livestock feed, and it smells of garlic.

Uncertain: Livestock feeding trials are thin. The limit is a caution based on its chemistry, not a list of poisoning cases.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit Uncertain

    Garlic mustard contains mustard oils and garlic-like compounds. It is not a documented staple feed, and Allium relatives cause blood damage in several species.

    Leave it out of the mix. Removing it from a woods is still worth doing; just do not feed the bag.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Heart-shaped toothed leaves, a garlic smell when crushed, and small white flowers with four petals in the second year.

Lookalikes

Violets do not smell of garlic. Ground ivy creeps and has scalloped round leaves.

Parts to feed

Not a recommended feed. Pulling it for disposal is a different job from feeding it.

New England timing

Rosettes overwinter. The best leaves are April and May, before the white flowers set seed. It is a serious New England woodland invasive.

Harvest

Do not add it to a forage basket.

Preparation

There is no preparation step that turns it into a recommended feed.

Sources

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Alternate glossy leaves with smooth edges, small pale flowers, and berries that turn from red to black. The bark, scraped, is yellow-orange inside. Common buckthorn has toothed leaves and often a thorn at the tip.

Lookalikes

Alder grows in the same wet places and is not a feed in this guide. Cherry smells like bitter almond. If you are looking at buckthorn, do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, bark, or berries.

New England timing

It leafs out early and keeps leaves late. It is an invasive shrub of New England wetlands and old fields. Common buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) gets the same verdict.

Harvest

Do not cut it for animals.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Identification

Scalloped round leaves on a creeping square stem, and purple flowers in the leaf axils. It smells minty when crushed.

Lookalikes

Violets have heart-shaped leaves and do not creep the same way. Garlic mustard smells of garlic and does not creep into a mat.

Parts to feed

Do not feed it.

New England timing

It is green in April and May and again in the cool fall, often under shrubs and in lawns.

Harvest

Do not add lawn mats of ground ivy to clippings.

Preparation

Drying is not a reason to feed it.

Legume Toxic to some animals Spring Summer

Vicia villosa

A climbing vetch that has poisoned cattle. It is not a cut-and-carry feed.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Chicken Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Duck Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Goose Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Turkey Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Quail Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Guinea pig Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Goat Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Sheep Toxic

    Sheep are also poisoned by hairy vetch. Do not feed it.

    Seeds and mature growth are the usual concern.

  • Pig Toxic Uncertain

    Hairy vetch has caused fever, skin disease, and death in cattle. It is not safe cut-and-carry forage for the other animals in this guide either.

    Remove it from mixed cuttings. Seeds are part of the problem.

  • Cattle Toxic

    Hairy vetch poisoning is documented in cattle after grazing or hay: dermatitis, systemic illness, and death.

    Do not feed it.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Hairy stems, purple pea flowers in one-sided clusters, and many small leaflets.

Lookalikes

Garden pea vines are hairless, with larger leaflets and tendrils on a plant you planted. Bird vetch is similar enough that a weedy vetch should not be fed.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, seeds, or hay made from it.

New England timing

A cover crop and roadside vine. It flowers in early summer. Poisoning cases are associated with grazing and with hay.

Harvest

Pull it out of a mixed bundle.

Preparation

Drying does not make hairy vetch safe.

Vaccinium corymbosum

A native shrub. The fruit is the part animals actually get. Leaves are not a bulk feed.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Ripe blueberries are an acceptable treat. The shrub is not a leaf forage, and it grows next to laurels that are toxic.

    Be sure the bush is blueberry before you pick. Do not feed leaves as the product.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

An upright shrub, alternate oval leaves, white urn-shaped flowers, and blue berries with a bloom.

Lookalikes

Sheep laurel has pink saucer flowers and opposite or whorled leaves and is deadly. If the shrub is evergreen with pink saucers, it is not blueberry.

Parts to feed

Ripe berries as a treat. Leaves only in a small accidental amount.

New England timing

Fruit ripens in July and August in most of New England, earlier on warm coastal sites, later in the mountains and in Maine.

Harvest

Pick berries. Do not cut the bushes for leaf fodder.

Preparation

Feed fruit fresh, in modest amounts. It is sugar, not a forage base.

Sources

Identification

Spiny stems and leaves, potato-like purple or white flowers, and yellow berries.

Lookalikes

Potato flowers look similar. Potato vines are toxic too. A spiny plant in the pasture with potato flowers is horsenettle.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or berries.

New England timing

It stands in New England pastures from June until frost, with yellow berries late in the season.

Harvest

Do not include it in a cutting.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Toxic parts

Toxic parts: Cornell lists all parts as poisonous. Iowa State Extension lists only the corms (tubers). We show the broader Cornell list.

  • Cornell University Department of Animal Science, Plants Poisonous to Livestock: Arisaema spp. (Jack in the Pulpit)
    Arisaema spp.. Species most often affected: humans. Poisonous parts: all. Primary poisons: oxalate.
  • NC State Extension, North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox: Arisaema triphyllum (Bog onion, Brown dragon, Common Jack-in-the-Pulpit, Devil's ear, Dragon root, Indian Cradle, Indian Jack in The Pulpit, Indian Turnip, Jack-in-the-pulpit, Lady-in-a-chaise, Lord-and-Lady, Memory root, Parson-in-the-Pulpit, Pepper turnip, Starch wort, Three-leaved indian turnip, Wake robin, Wild turnip)
    Poisonous to humans. Poison severity: Low. Poison part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Toxic principle: Calcium oxalate crystals.

Do not feed it to them. Details are under Who can eat it.

Identification

One or two leaves, each with three leaflets, and a hooded flower (the spathe) around a club (the spadix).

Lookalikes

Trillium also has parts in threes but the flower is not a hooded jack. If you are looking at a hooded flower in the woods, do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, corm, or berries.

New England timing

It is up in New England woods in May and June. The red fruit cluster comes later and is not feed.

Harvest

Do not dig or cut it for animals.

Preparation

Drying does not make the crystals a reason to experiment.

Identification

Large toothed leaves, a foul smell, white or pale purple trumpet flowers, and a spiny egg-shaped pod.

Lookalikes

Ground cherry has a papery husk and is not a reason to experiment. If the plant has a spiny pod and a trumpet flower, do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, flowers, or seeds.

New England timing

It appears in New England barnyards and gardens in midsummer and carries spiny pods into frost.

Harvest

Pull it away from pens. Do not put it in the feed.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Garden Spring Summer Fall Winter

Brassica oleracea · cabbage leaves, collards, broccoli leaves

A cold-hardy garden brassica. Gas and goitrogens are the limit, and kale anemia is a cattle problem when the intake is high.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Safe

    House Rabbit Society lists kale (all types) among the leafy greens that are safe for rabbits. Introduce it slowly, like any new green.

    A leaf or two for a rabbit, or a small share of a mix, is the usual limit. Do not switch cattle onto a field of kale all at once.

  • Chicken Limit

    Brassicas cause gas in rabbits and can cause anemia and thyroid trouble in ruminants when they become a large share of the diet.

    A leaf or two for a rabbit, or a small share of a mix, is the usual limit. Do not switch cattle onto a field of kale all at once.

  • Duck Limit Uncertain

    Brassicas cause gas in rabbits and can cause anemia and thyroid trouble in ruminants when they become a large share of the diet.

    A leaf or two for a rabbit, or a small share of a mix, is the usual limit. Do not switch cattle onto a field of kale all at once. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A duck-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Goose Limit Uncertain

  • Guinea pig Limit Uncertain

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Blue-green curly or flat leaves on a plant you planted. Broccoli and cabbage leaves count as this entry.

Lookalikes

Comfrey is hairy with bell flowers and is toxic. Do not grab a large garden leaf without knowing it.

Parts to feed

Leaves, in moderation.

New England timing

Spring plantings are cut from June. Fall plantings hold into November and, in southern New England, through many winters. Cabbage, collards, and broccoli leaves are the same species and the same limit.

Harvest

Cut leaves, not a wheelbarrow of them for a few rabbits.

Preparation

Feed fresh and limited. Do not feed a sudden large amount to cattle or sheep.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A boat-shaped leaf tip and a fine, dark green sod. The flower head is an open pyramid.

Lookalikes

Annual bluegrass is paler and seeds low to the ground. Quackgrass has clasping auricles at the leaf base.

Parts to feed

Leaves. Skip seed heads once they are dry and stemmy.

New England timing

It greens up in April and May and grows again in the cool fall. It stalls in hot, dry July weather.

Harvest

Only cut plants you know have not been treated with lawn herbicide or insecticide.

Preparation

Feed small amounts fresh, or dry them. Lawn clippings heat and mold quickly, so feed them the same day or not at all.

Forb Summer

Chenopodium album

A common garden weed. Poultry and pigs eat it. Nitrate and oxalate set the limit.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Diamond-shaped leaves with a white mealy coating, especially on the growing tips.

Lookalikes

Pigweed (Amaranthus) has a coarser stem and no white meal on the tip. Nightshades have different flowers and berries and are toxic.

Parts to feed

Young tops only, and not from heavily fertilized ground.

New England timing

From June until it goes to seed in late summer. Plants on rich garden soil can accumulate nitrate.

Harvest

Cut young plants. Skip thick stands on old manure piles.

Preparation

Feed a limited fresh amount. Do not ferment a large mass of it.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

The plant you sowed: a head or loose leaves, milky sap when the stem is cut, and no strong odor.

Lookalikes

Wild lettuce is a different, more bitter plant and is not given the same verdict here. Feed the garden plant you know.

Parts to feed

Leaves. Not a diet of it.

New England timing

Garden lettuce is cut from May until a hard frost if it is replanted. It bolts and turns bitter in July heat.

Harvest

Cut outer leaves or a whole head you grew or bought. Wash it.

Preparation

Feed fresh. Do not feed spoiled, slimy leaves. Iceberg is poor nutrition and is the one to skip.

Identification

Two broad basal leaves and a one-sided stalk of small white bells, then red berries.

Lookalikes

Wild lily of the valley (Maianthemum) is a smaller woodland plant and is not a feed either. Ramps smell strongly of onion and are an Allium, which is its own toxic entry.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, flowers, berries, or roots.

New England timing

It flowers in May in New England shade gardens and persists as a groundcover. Leaves and rhizomes are present through the summer.

Harvest

Do not pull the patch for animals.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Identification

A taller evergreen shrub, glossy alternate leaves, and terminal clusters of pink or white saucer flowers with ten pockets.

Lookalikes

Rhododendron and azalea are in the same toxic group. Sheep laurel is lower and flowers along the stem. Do not feed any of them.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or clippings.

New England timing

It flowers in June. It is common in Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts and present in southern parts of the northern states. Leaves are toxic whenever they are green.

Harvest

Do not dump prunings where stock can reach them.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Browse Spring Summer Fall

Rosa multiflora

An invasive rose. Goats are often used to knock it back. The leaves are browse, not a poisonous plant.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    The leaves are edible browse, not a toxic plant. Thorns and the way it tangles wool and hides poison ivy are the practical limits.

    A goat will take more of it than a rabbit or a sheep should be asked to.

  • Chicken Limit

    The leaves are edible browse, not a toxic plant. Thorns and the way it tangles wool and hides poison ivy are the practical limits.

    A goat will take more of it than a rabbit or a sheep should be asked to.

  • Duck Limit Uncertain

    A goat will take more of it than a rabbit or a sheep should be asked to. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A quail-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Guinea pig Limit Uncertain

    The leaves are edible browse, not a toxic plant. Thorns and the way it tangles wool and hides poison ivy are the practical limits.

    A goat will take more of it than a rabbit or a sheep should be asked to. Guinea-pig trials for this plant are limited, so this follows the rabbit verdict and is marked uncertain.

  • Goat Safe

    Goats readily browse multiflora rose and are used to suppress it. The plant is not a toxin problem for them.

    Thorns still injure udders and the person cutting canes. Check the patch for poison ivy.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Arching canes, fringed stipules at the leaf base, clusters of small white flowers, then small red hips. Thorns are recurved.

Lookalikes

Blackberry has aggregate fruit, not a hip. Native roses are not a reason to skip identification, but the feeding note is similar if you are sure it is a rose and not a bramble mixed with poison ivy.

Parts to feed

Leaves and young tips. Hips are not the main feed.

New England timing

Leaves from May until frost. White flower clusters in June. It is a widespread New England invasive.

Harvest

Cut tips with heavy gloves. It will take over a field if you only cut a little and leave the crowns.

Preparation

Feed fresh. Thorns are the limit, especially for sheep because of the wool.

Sources

  • Background reading: Langston University, E (Kika) de la Garza American Institute for Goat Research, goat nutrition materials.
  • Background reading: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.
  • Background reading: University of Maine Cooperative Extension, forage guidance.

Allium cepa · garlic, chives, leeks

An Allium. It causes red-blood-cell damage. It does not belong in a forage basket.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Onions, garlic, chives, and leeks contain compounds that damage red blood cells. Cattle, sheep, goats, and poultry are affected. Rabbits should not get them either.

    Do not feed kitchen scraps of onion or garlic.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Hollow or flat blue-green leaves in a bulb you planted, with the familiar onion smell.

Lookalikes

Garlic mustard smells of garlic but is a broad-leaved invasive. Both stay out of the feed.

Parts to feed

Do not feed bulbs, leaves, or trimmings.

New England timing

Garden onions are pulled in late summer. Chives, garlic, and leeks are the same refusal all season.

Harvest

Do not dump kitchen onion scraps into the poultry pen or the rabbit greens.

Preparation

Cooking is not a step that makes a pile of onions into forage.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Clumped plant with a flattened stem base. The flower head is branched, with clumps of spikelets, not a single tight cylinder.

Lookalikes

Timothy has one dense cylindrical head. Tall fescue has a coarser leaf and often reddish stem bases.

Parts to feed

Leaves and stems.

New England timing

Leaves are usable from May into October. The bunched seed heads show in late May and June. Later growth stays leafy if it is cut before it gets coarse.

Harvest

Cut leaf growth and leave the crown. Older stems are poor feed.

Preparation

Feed fresh or as hay. Discard moldy material.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Broad oval leaves with parallel veins, in a rosette. The flower is a green spike. English plantain has lance leaves and a similar spike.

Lookalikes

Some lilies send up strap leaves, but they lack the parallel-veined rosette and the green spike. If the plant is not clearly plantain, leave it.

Parts to feed

Leaves of both common and English plantain.

New England timing

Leaves are usable from May until frost. They get stringy in late summer. English plantain (Plantago lanceolata) is the narrow-leaved relative and is used the same way.

Harvest

Cut leaves, not the tough flower spikes. Avoid sprayed lawns.

Preparation

Feed fresh or dried. No special wilting.

Sources

  • Background reading: House Rabbit Society, suggested greens and foods to avoid.
  • Background reading: ATTRA / NCAT, poultry and small-ruminant forage publications.
  • Background reading: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service plant guide.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairless stem with purple spots, finely divided parsley-like leaves, a musty smell, and white umbrella-shaped flower clusters.

Lookalikes

Queen Anne's lace has a hairy stem and smells like carrot. Water hemlock grows in wetter ground and has chambered roots. If you are not sure, do not cut any of them.

Parts to feed

Do not feed any part, including the root.

New England timing

Rosettes are green in spring. Tall spotted stems and white flowers appear in June and July along New England roads, ditches, and waste ground.

Harvest

Do not put it in a basket. Do not compost it into a pen.

Preparation

There is no drying or cooking step in this guide that makes it feed.

Colorado State University and the University of Arkansas Extension say animals are unaffected by poison ivy. We keep it cautious because the oil on coats and in manure harms the people who handle them, and we found no source that confirms it is safe feed for every animal listed here.

  • Colorado State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Guide to Poisonous Plants: Poison ivy (Toxicodendron radicans (L.) Kuntze)
    Animals affected: Animals are not affected by poison ivy. People are primarily sensitive to the irritant oil in the plant. Toxic principle: The leaves and stems contain an irritant oil called urushiol that is released from the crushed or broken surface of the leaves or stems. Special notes: Poison ivy is usually not a…
  • University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service: Plants Poisonous to Livestock in the Southern US
    Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron radicans) • Toxic Principle: phenolic compound urushiol • Mucous and membrane irritant • No effect on livestock. • Breathing smoke may cause irritation.

Do not feed it to them. Details are under Who can eat it.

Browse Toxic to some animals Spring Summer Fall

Toxicodendron radicans

Not a cut-and-carry plant. The person cutting it is the one who gets hurt. Goats often eat it and are a special case below.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed.

  • Chicken Toxic

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed.

  • Duck Toxic Uncertain

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A duck-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Goose Toxic Uncertain

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A goose-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Turkey Toxic Uncertain

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A turkey-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Quail Toxic Uncertain

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A quail-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Guinea pig Toxic Uncertain

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed. Guinea-pig trials for this plant are limited, so this follows the rabbit verdict and is marked uncertain.

  • Goat Limit

    Goats browse poison ivy readily and are used to clear it. Kept at limit because the sources disagree on caution. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not harvest it to carry to goats. If they eat it on their own, that is not an invitation to cut more.

  • Sheep Toxic

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed.

  • Pig Toxic

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed.

  • Cattle Toxic

    Kept cautious. Colorado State and Arkansas Extension say livestock are not affected, but we have not found a source that clears poison ivy as feed for each animal here. The oil, urushiol, stays on coats and in manure and blisters people who handle them.

    Do not touch it. Do not put it in the feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Three leaflets, the center one on a longer stalk, often shiny, and a woody vine or low shrub. White berries late in the year. No thorns.

Lookalikes

Virginia creeper usually has five leaflets. Blackberry has thorns and five leaflets. Raspberry has thorns. When in doubt, do not touch it.

Parts to feed

Do not cut it by hand for any animal.

New England timing

It leafs out in May and is a handling hazard until the leaves are gone. Vines and low plants are both common across New England.

Harvest

Do not put it in a basket, a wheelbarrow of greens, or a hay pile.

Preparation

There is no safe handling method offered here.

Phytolacca americana

A tall native plant of New England edges and gardens. It is poisonous. The berries stain and tempt people who have heard they are food.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Phytolaccatoxin and related compounds. The root is the most dangerous part. Leaves and berries poison livestock too.

    Do not feed it. Do not treat the purple berries as a poultry treat.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Large alternate leaves, a red-purple stem, and drooping clusters of dark purple berries. The plant can be taller than a person.

Lookalikes

Elderberry is a woody shrub with opposite leaves and red-purple stems on a bush, not this herb. Neither is a safe leafy feed.

Parts to feed

Do not feed shoots, leaves, berries, or roots.

New England timing

Shoots come up in May. Berries ripen purple in late summer and fall. The root is the most toxic part and is present all season.

Harvest

Do not cut it for a basket.

Preparation

No livestock preparation makes pokeweed feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Compound leaves on a plant you planted, white or purple flowers, and tubers underground.

Lookalikes

Tomato vines are hairier and smell stronger. Horsenettle is spiny. All three are toxic.

Parts to feed

Do not feed vines, green tubers, or sprouted green skin.

New England timing

Vines are green from June until they die back. Green tubers show up at harvest, late summer and fall.

Harvest

Do not throw the pulled vines to livestock.

Preparation

No preparation in this guide turns the vine into feed.

Forb Summer

Portulaca oleracea

A succulent garden weed. Poultry take it readily. Oxalate is the limit.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Purslane is a useful green and also an oxalate plant. Large amounts are a poor idea for rabbits, guinea pigs, and ruminants, and unnecessary for poultry.

    A small share of a summer mix is the usual place for it.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Thick red stems, fleshy oval leaves, and small yellow flowers. The plant sprawls.

Lookalikes

Spurge has milky sap and is not purslane. If the broken stem bleeds white latex, do not feed it.

Parts to feed

Stems and leaves, in moderation.

New England timing

A heat weed. In New England it is worth cutting from July until frost, mostly in gardens and bare soil.

Harvest

Cut above the soil. Confirm there is no milky sap.

Preparation

Feed fresh. Do not make it the whole basket, because of oxalate.

A poplar used as browse. Bigtooth aspen is similar. Bark in large amounts is the part to avoid.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Rounded leaves that tremble, flattened leaf stalks, and smooth pale bark on young trees.

Lookalikes

Birch has a different bark and toothed leaves that do not tremble on flat stalks. Cherry smells like bitter almond when a twig is scratched.

Parts to feed

Leaves and small twigs. Not slabs of bark.

New England timing

Twigs and young leaves from late spring through summer. Winter twigs are browse when the leaves are gone. It is common in northern New England.

Harvest

Cut small branches. Do not strip a trunk.

Preparation

Feed fresh. A normal browse portion, not a diet of bark.

Sources

Daucus carota · wild carrot

Wild carrot. The plant itself is a minor green. The emergency is mistaking poison hemlock or water hemlock for it.

Uncertain: Do not harvest white umbels unless the hairy stem and carrot smell are obvious.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    A correctly identified wild carrot is a carrot relative, not a hemlock. The limit stands because a mistake is fatal and because some umbels are phototoxic.

    If the stem is hairless or purple-spotted, or the plant is in standing water, stop. That is not this entry.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairy stem, a carrot smell, white flat flower clusters often with one dark floret in the center, and a nest-like seed head that curls inward.

Lookalikes

Poison hemlock is hairless, with purple spots on the stem and a musty smell. Water hemlock grows in wet ground, is hairless, and has chambered roots. If the stem is smooth, do not call it Queen Anne's lace.

Parts to feed

Only a correctly identified plant, and only a small amount of leaf. When there is any doubt, feed none of it.

New England timing

White flowers in July and August. The first-year rosette is around earlier. The identification risk is highest when only leaves are present.

Harvest

If you cannot separate it from hemlock with certainty, do not cut umbels at all.

Preparation

There is no preparation that fixes a wrong identification.

Legume Spring Summer

Trifolium pratense

A hay and pasture clover, upright, with pink-purple heads.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Red clover shares the bloat risk of other clovers. It also contains phytoestrogens. A leaf fungus (black patch) is tied to slobbers, which is saliva and irritation best known in horses.

    Use a small share of a mix. Do not feed blotched, moldy clover.

Identification

Three leaflets with a pale mark, hairy stems, and a pink head sitting close to the upper leaves.

Lookalikes

Alsike clover is finer, not hairy, with a pink-and-white head. White clover creeps.

Parts to feed

Leaves and young flower heads, sparingly.

New England timing

Cut leaf and early flower from June into August. Plants with brown patches on the leaves may carry the fungus associated with slobbers.

Harvest

Skip plants with lots of brown leaf blotches. Do not make it the whole cutting.

Preparation

Wilt before feeding ruminants. Dry hay is safer than lush wet clover. Discard mold.

Acer rubrum

A common swamp and yard maple. Wilted leaves cause red-blood-cell destruction, best documented in horses.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Opposite leaves with sharper teeth than a sugar maple, red buds and often red leaf stalks, and red fall color. It tolerates wet ground.

Lookalikes

Sugar maple has smoother lobes and brown buds. If you cannot tell them apart, feed neither. Oak leaves are alternate, not opposite.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves. Do not feed wilted branch prunings.

New England timing

The dangerous New England window is wilted or fallen leaves, especially after a storm and in September and October. Spring leaves are not a feed either.

Harvest

Do not toss storm-downed maple limbs into a pen.

Preparation

Drying and wilting are the problem, not the cure.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Upright canes with a whitish bloom, leaves usually in threes, and a red fruit that slips off the core.

Lookalikes

Blackberry fruit keeps its core. Wineberry, an invasive, has red hairs on the cane. Wineberry leaves are not a separate entry; do not assume every cane is raspberry.

Parts to feed

Leaves and tender tips. Ripe fruit as a small treat for poultry and pigs.

New England timing

Leaves from May through August. Fruit in July in southern New England, later north.

Harvest

Cut leafy tips, not the whole cane.

Preparation

Fresh or dried leaves. No special wilting.

Forb Summer

Amaranthus retroflexus

A coarse garden and barnyard weed. Nitrate is the hazard.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Pigweed is a nitrate accumulator. Cattle have been poisoned by large amounts of stressed plants. Smaller species should not get a heavy feeding either.

    A few young leaves in a mix are a different risk from a trough of pigweed. When in doubt, leave the stand.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A red taproot, oval leaves, and a bristly green flower cluster. The stem is rough.

Lookalikes

Lambsquarters has a white mealy tip. Spiny amaranth has sharp spines and should be left alone.

Parts to feed

Young leaves, if at all, and never a cartload from rich ground.

New England timing

Midsummer into early fall. Nitrate is highest in stressed or heavily fertilized plants, which are common in gardens and barnyards.

Harvest

Skip plants that were drought-stressed and then heavily manured.

Preparation

There is no home preparation that removes nitrate.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Broad leaves and a straw-colored, open seed head. It forms dense stands in wet soil. Ligule is prominent.

Lookalikes

Orchardgrass is an upland clump grass. Reed canarygrass is wetter and taller.

Parts to feed

Young leaves only, and only in a mix.

New England timing

It is up early in wet ground, from May, and is coarse by July. Older varieties contain alkaloids. Low-alkaloid varieties exist and look the same.

Harvest

Cut before it becomes a coarse cane. Leave the wet roots alone.

Preparation

Hay from high-alkaloid stands is still a poor feed. Do not assume drying makes it safe.

Rhododendron spp. · azalea, great laurel

A common yard shrub and a native evergreen. Grayanotoxins make the leaves poisonous.

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Grayanotoxins in rhododendron and azalea leaves cause vomiting, collapse, and death in livestock. Goats are often the animal that eats yard trimmings.

    Do not feed clippings.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Evergreen leathery leaves in whorls, or deciduous azalea leaves, and showy tubular flowers. Garden azaleas count.

Lookalikes

Mountain laurel has saucer flowers with pockets. Both are toxic. Do not feed either.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, flowers, or clippings.

New England timing

Garden azaleas and rhododendrons flower in May and June. Great laurel (Rhododendron maximum) is native in southern New England. Leaves are toxic all year.

Harvest

Do not throw hedge trimmings to goats.

Preparation

Honey from a heavy rhododendron flow is a human hazard. It is not animal feed either.

Rheum rhabarbarum

A perennial garden plant. The leaf blade is an oxalate poison. This guide does not recommend the stalks for animals either.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Huge heart-shaped leaves on thick red or green stalks, dying back in winter.

Lookalikes

Swiss chard has a thick midrib but a smaller leaf and is a row crop. Burdock is hairy. If the plant is the rhubarb clump, do not feed the leaf.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves. Do not feed stalks as forage.

New England timing

Stalks are pulled in May and June in New England. The leaves are toxic then and for the rest of the summer.

Harvest

Do not toss the pulled leaves into a pen.

Preparation

No preparation makes the leaf safe.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A low evergreen shrub, opposite or whorled narrow leaves, and clusters of pink flowers along the stem, not only at the tip.

Lookalikes

Mountain laurel is taller, with flowers in a terminal cluster. Both are toxic. Blueberry has alternate leaves and a blueberry flower, not a Kalmia saucer.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or flowers.

New England timing

It blooms pink in June on New England barrens, pastures, and bog edges. The leaves are toxic all season. The old name lambkill is literal.

Harvest

Do not browse a pasture shrub that looks like this.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Identification

A mottled purple-brown hood in very early spring, then large oval leaves from the mud. Torn leaves smell skunky.

Lookalikes

False hellebore is taller, with pleated leaves up a stem, in wet meadows. Both are toxic.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or roots.

New England timing

The spotted hood appears in early spring, sometimes through snow, in New England swamps. Huge leaves follow in May and June.

Harvest

Do not cut a swamp plant that smells like skunk.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairless grass with a drooping, open flower head and a small M-shaped watermark on some young leaves.

Lookalikes

Orchardgrass is clumped and the stem base is flattened. Quackgrass has auricles that clasp the stem.

Parts to feed

Leaves and stems as hay or fresh cut.

New England timing

Best leaf is in May and June. It is cut for hay in early summer. Regrowth is modest in a dry August.

Harvest

Cut at early heading. Mature stems are low quality.

Preparation

Dry fully for hay, or feed fresh in a mix. Discard mold.

Tree Summer Fall

Rhus typhina

A red-fruited sumac. It is not poison sumac. Feeding data are thinner than the identification difference, so the verdict stays limited.

Uncertain: The toxicology of staghorn sumac as a feed is thin. The poison-sumac distinction is not.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit Uncertain

    Staghorn sumac is not poison sumac, and goats browse it. It is still a limited feed because a white-berried sumac in a wetland is a different, more dangerous plant, and because this shrub is not a studied staple.

    If the berries are white or the shrubs are standing in a bog, do not cut them.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Fuzzy twigs, compound leaves with many leaflets, and upright red fuzzy fruit clusters.

Lookalikes

Poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix) grows in wetlands, has smooth twigs, and bears drooping white berries. If the fruit is white, or the ground is a bog, stop.

Parts to feed

Leaves only if you are certain this is staghorn sumac. Not a staple.

New England timing

Leaves from June until they redden in September. Red fruit clusters persist into winter. It is a common New England roadside shrub.

Harvest

Do not harvest any sumac with white berries. Do not harvest in a swamp.

Preparation

There is no preparation that fixes a mix-up with poison sumac.

Sources

Forb Spring Summer

Urtica dioica

A mineral-rich green that stings until it is wilted or dried.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Safe

    Wilted or dried nettle is a traditional livestock and rabbit green. The sting is mechanical and is gone once the hairs are dried or thoroughly wilted.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Opposite, toothed, heart-shaped leaves and square stems covered in stinging hairs. It grows in damp, rich soil.

Lookalikes

Deadnettle and henbit do not sting. Wood nettle has alternate leaves. If you are not sure, do not grab it.

Parts to feed

Young tops, after the sting is removed by wilting or drying.

New England timing

Cut in May and June before it flowers. By July the stems are fibrous. Wood nettle is a woodland relative and is not this feed.

Harvest

Cut with gloves. Do not rub the plant into skin.

Preparation

Wilt until the leaves are limp, or dry them fully, before they are feed. Fresh unwilted nettle stings mouths.

Acer saccharum

Not the classic red-maple poisoning tree, and still not a leaf to mix up with red maple.

Uncertain: Sugar maple leaves have much less published poisoning data than red maple. The limit is there because the two trees are confused and because leaves are an unneeded risk.

    Sugar maple is not the species in the classic wilted-leaf poisoning, which is red maple. Leaves are still a poor feed and are easy to confuse with red maple.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Opposite leaves with smoother, rounded sinuses and pointed lobes. Buds are brown and sharp. Older bark is plated.

Lookalikes

Red maple has sharper teeth, red buds, and often a wetter site. Feed neither if you cannot separate them.

Parts to feed

Small winter twigs only, and only when you are sure the tree is sugar maple. Not a pile of leaves.

New England timing

Leaves are on the tree from May to October. Winter twigs are what people actually offer. It is a dominant tree in northern New England woods.

Harvest

Do not feed fallen leaves. Do not feed storm-wilted branches.

Preparation

There is no reason to dry the leaves for feed.

Sources

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Large shiny leaves with a thick white, yellow, or red midrib, on a plant you planted. Beet leaves count.

Lookalikes

Rhubarb also has a thick stalk, and the leaf is toxic. Rhubarb leaves are broader and the plant is a large clump that dies to the ground. Do not mix them up.

Parts to feed

Leaves, sparingly.

New England timing

Leaves are cut from July until frost. Beet greens are the same plant species and the same oxalate limit.

Harvest

Cut a few leaves, not a daily diet of chard.

Preparation

Feed fresh and limited. Drying does not remove oxalate.

Sources

Grass Spring Summer Fall

Lolium arundinaceum · Schedonorus arundinaceus

A tough pasture grass. The endophyte, not the leaf shape, is the feeding problem.

Uncertain: Endophyte status of a given plant cannot be judged by eye.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit Uncertain

    Tall fescue endophyte produces ergovaline. In cattle and sheep it is tied to heat stress, poor gain, and reproductive trouble. You cannot see the infection.

    A little in a mixed pasture is common. Do not feed a heavy stand as the only forage. Endophyte-free and novel-endophyte varieties exist, but a plant in a field does not show which it is.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Coarse dark leaves, prominent veins, and often a reddish base. It grows in clumps.

Lookalikes

Orchardgrass has a flattened stem and a branched seed head. Reed canarygrass prefers wetter soil and has a more open seed head.

Parts to feed

Leaves, if you use it at all. Do not make a suspect stand the whole diet.

New England timing

It grows from May through October and stays green late. Many older New England pastures are endophyte-infected. The fungus is invisible.

Harvest

If you cut it, keep the amount small and mix it with other forage.

Preparation

Drying does not remove the endophyte toxin.

Forb Toxic to some animals Summer

Jacobaea vulgaris · Senecio jacobaea

A pyrrolizidine-alkaloid ragwort. Liver damage is cumulative.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Pyrrolizidine alkaloids cause irreversible liver damage. Cattle and horses are very sensitive. Goats and sheep are somewhat more resistant and are still not animals to feed this plant to.

    Do not use resistance as a reason to cut ragwort for goats.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A biennial with a ragged yellow flower cluster and deeply lobed leaves. The plant is coarse and bitter.

Lookalikes

Tansy (Tanacetum) has button flowers and is also not a feed. Goldenrods have different flower heads. Do not feed a yellow late-summer weed on a guess.

Parts to feed

Do not feed fresh plants or hay that contains them.

New England timing

It flowers in mid to late summer in New England pastures and on disturbed ground. The alkaloid remains in hay.

Harvest

Pull it out of a cutting.

Preparation

Drying does not remove the alkaloids.

Phleum pratense · herd's grass

A standard cool-season hay grass of New England fields.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Safe

    A standard hay grass with no important toxin in normal stands.

    Use it as fiber or as one green in a mix. It does not replace a complete feed for birds or pigs.

  • Chicken Safe

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A dense, cylindrical seed head like a small bottle brush. The stem base has a small swollen corm. The shoot is rolled.

Lookalikes

Orchardgrass grows in clumps and has a more open flower head. Reed canarygrass is taller and prefers wetter ground.

Parts to feed

Leaves and fine stems, fresh or as hay.

New England timing

Growth starts in May. The main hay cut in New England is often in June, with a second growth through August. Quality falls once the seed head is mature.

Harvest

Cut above the crown and leave stubble. Skip roadsides and any field sprayed with herbicide.

Preparation

Feed fresh in a mix, or dry it fully. Do not feed moldy hay.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairy, strong-smelling vine you planted, with yellow flowers and green fruit that ripens red, yellow, or another ripe color.

Lookalikes

Horsenettle is spiny and wild. Potato vines are a separate toxic entry. Do not feed any of them.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves, stems, or green fruit.

New England timing

Vines are up from June until frost. Green fruit and leaves are the problem all season. Ripe fruit is late summer.

Harvest

Do not toss suckers and prunings into a pen.

Preparation

Ripe red fruit, seeds and all, is sometimes a small treat for chickens and pigs. It is not forage, and it is not a rabbit food in this guide.

Identification

Five leaflets from one point, and a vine that climbs with adhesive disks. Berries are dark blue on red stalks.

Lookalikes

Poison ivy has three leaflets. If you see three, stop and do not touch it. Five leaflets point here, which is still not a feed.

Parts to feed

Do not feed leaves or berries.

New England timing

It covers New England fences and woods edges from June until the leaves turn red in September. Berries ripen dark in the fall.

Harvest

Do not pull it down into a pen as browse.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A hairless, sometimes purple-streaked stem, divided leaves, white flower clusters, and a wet-ground habit. The root, cut lengthwise, shows chambers.

Lookalikes

Poison hemlock is the upland spotted plant. Angelica and other white umbels are not safe guesses. Do not dig wet-ground parsleys.

Parts to feed

Do not feed roots, stems, or leaves.

New England timing

It grows in New England marshes, ditches, and wet meadows and is dangerous from the time it leafs out in May until it dies back.

Harvest

Do not pull it for feed. The root is especially dangerous.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Compound leaves, a small cluster of white flowers, then white berries on thick red stalks, each berry with a black dot. Red baneberry has red berries.

Lookalikes

False Solomon's seal has a different flower cluster and is not a feed in this guide. Do not feed woodland berries to animals.

Parts to feed

Do not feed berries, roots, or leaves.

New England timing

It flowers in late spring in rich New England woods. The white berries with black dots, doll's eyes, are obvious later in summer. Red baneberry (Actaea rubra) gets the same verdict.

Harvest

Do not gather it.

Preparation

No preparation makes it feed.

Legume Spring Summer Fall

Trifolium repens

The common clover of New England lawns and pastures.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Lush clover causes frothy bloat in cattle, sheep, and goats. Rabbits and guinea pigs bloat or get soft stools from too much clover. A cyanide concern also appears in stressed or wilted clover.

    A small handful in a mixed bundle is the usual limit. Do not feed a clover-only cutting to ruminants.

  • Chicken Limit
