Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Three leaflets, often with a pale crescent, and a white flower head on a leafless stalk. It creeps and roots at the nodes.

Lookalikes

Red clover is upright with a pink head. Alsike clover has a pink-and-white head and no crescent mark. Wood sorrel has heart-shaped leaflets and a sour taste.

Parts to feed

Leaves and flowers, in limited amounts.

New England timing

It flowers from June into September. The lush May and June growth is the highest bloat risk for ruminants.

Harvest

Pick from places that are not sprayed. Do not harvest a pure stand as the only feed for goats, sheep, or cattle.

Preparation

Wilt it a little for ruminants to reduce bloat. Fresh small amounts are the usual rabbit and poultry use. Moldy clover is not feed.

Morus alba

One of the better tree leaves for rabbits and goats.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Alternate leaves, variously lobed or heart-shaped, often on the same tree, with milky sap and a berry that looks like a pale blackberry.

Lookalikes

Basswood leaves are larger and heart-shaped without the mixed lobes, and the sap is not milky. White snakeroot is a short herb, not a tree.

Parts to feed

Leaves. Ripe fruit is a small treat for poultry and pigs.

New England timing

Leaves from late May through September. Fruit in early summer. It is a common invasive tree in southern and coastal New England and is planted elsewhere in the region.

Harvest

Clip leafy twigs. The milky sap is normal for mulberry and is not the milkweed warning.

Preparation

Feed fresh or dry the leaves. No wilting step is required.

Tree Toxic to some animals Spring Fall

Quercus alba

Oaks are common in southern and central New England and in warmer pockets north. Tannins are the problem.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop.

  • Chicken Limit

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop.

  • Duck Limit Uncertain

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A duck-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Goose Limit Uncertain

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A goose-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Turkey Limit Uncertain

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A turkey-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Quail Limit Uncertain

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop. This follows poultry guidance used for chickens. A quail-specific reference was not used, so it is marked uncertain.

  • Guinea pig Limit Uncertain

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop. Guinea-pig trials for this plant are limited, so this follows the rabbit verdict and is marked uncertain.

  • Goat Limit

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop.

  • Sheep Toxic

    Sheep are poisoned by the same oak tannins that affect cattle, especially on a heavy acorn drop.

    Do not feed acorns or young leaves.

  • Pig Limit

    Oak buds, young leaves, and acorns are high in tannins. They cause gut and kidney disease when they become a large part of the diet.

    A mouthful of mature leaf is not the same as a diet of acorns. Do not feed acorns as a crop.

  • Cattle Toxic

    Cattle are regularly poisoned by acorns and young oak leaves. Kidney damage and constipation or diarrhea are the picture.

    Keep cattle off a heavy acorn crop and do not feed oak cuttings.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Alternate lobed leaves. White oak has rounded lobes. Red oak has pointed lobes. Acorns sit in a cap.

Lookalikes

Maple leaves are opposite. Beech has smooth bark and a simple toothless leaf edge that is not lobed like an oak.

Parts to feed

Not young leaves, and not a meal of acorns.

New England timing

Young leaves in May and June and acorns in September and October are the risky parts. Red oaks (pointed lobes) are often worse than white oaks. Both are limited here.

Harvest

Do not shake a tree full of green acorns into a pen.

Preparation

There is no home step that removes tannins from a pile of acorns.

Forb Toxic to some animals Summer Fall

Ageratina altissima

A woodland plant that poisons animals and can poison people who drink the milk of animals that ate it.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Tremetol in white snakeroot causes trembles in cattle and other livestock, and the toxin passes into milk.

    Do not feed it. Keep lactating animals off it.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Opposite leaves with three main veins and toothed edges, and flat clusters of white flower heads. It grows in shade.

Lookalikes

Boneset has leaves that the stem appears to grow through. Late white woodland flowers should not be fed on a guess.

Parts to feed

Do not feed any part.

New England timing

It flowers in late summer and fall in New England woods and edges. The toxin passes into milk, which is the historical milk-sickness story.

Harvest

Do not add it to browse from a woods edge.

Preparation

Drying does not make it safe. Do not use the milk of an animal that may have eaten it.

A tall yellow umbel. The plant is phototoxic to stock and to the person cutting it.

  • Rabbit Toxic

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

A grooved stem, pinnate leaves, and flat yellow flower clusters. It is a biennial, with a rosette the first year.

Lookalikes

Golden alexanders bloom earlier and are smaller. Queen Anne's lace has white flowers. Poison hemlock has white flowers and purple-spotted stems.

Parts to feed

Do not feed any part. Do not get sap on skin.

New England timing

It flowers on New England roadsides in July and August. Sap on skin plus sunlight causes severe burns in people. That is a harvest hazard, not only a feeding one.

Harvest

If you must handle it, cover skin and wash off sap. Do not put it in the feed basket.

Preparation

There is no safe preparation for feed.

A standard browse for rabbits and goats. Salicylates are the reason not to feed a diet of bark.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Alternate, narrow leaves on flexible twigs, often along water. Buds are covered by a single scale.

Lookalikes

Brittle willow lookalikes are still willows. Cherry twigs have a bitter-almond smell when scratched and are a different, toxic entry.

Parts to feed

Twigs and leaves, in moderation. Not a pile of bark.

New England timing

Twigs are cut from late winter through summer. Pussy willow (Salix discolor) and black willow (Salix nigra) are common New England species. Leaves are best before midsummer.

Harvest

Cut finger-thick twigs. Do not girdle a tree you want to keep.

Preparation

Feed fresh. Dried leafy twigs are fine. Do not feed a large amount of bark.

Sources

Legume Summer

Melilotus officinalis · white sweet clover is the same caution

A tall roadside legume. Moldy sweet-clover hay causes a clotting failure.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Limit

    Moldy sweet clover makes dicoumarol, which stops blood from clotting. Cattle are the classic victims. Fresh, unspoiled plants do not have that toxin, but they are not a chosen staple.

    If the cutting smells moldy or heated, do not feed it to any animal.

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Tall, branched, with small yellow flowers in narrow clusters and a sweet smell when crushed. Leaves are in threes.

Lookalikes

White sweet clover is the same problem with white flowers. Alfalfa has purple flowers and does not smell the same.

Parts to feed

Not a preferred fresh feed. Spoiled hay is dangerous.

New England timing

Tall plants flower along New England roadsides in July and August. The bleeding problem is in spoiled hay, not in a fresh handful.

Harvest

Do not bale it wet. Do not feed stems that heated or molded.

Preparation

Fresh plants are a limited green. Any moldy sweet-clover hay should be thrown out, not diluted.

Taxus canadensis · Japanese yew, English yew, Taxus cuspidata, Taxus baccata

Yew is extremely poisonous. A handful of clippings can kill.

Who can eat it

  • Rabbit Toxic

    Taxine alkaloids. Yew causes sudden death in livestock. Canada yew and the cultivated yews are all dangerous. The red cup does not make the seed or the needles safe.

    Do not feed any part. Do not compost clippings where animals can reach them.

  • Chicken Toxic

Not yet sourced: summary, identification, lookalikes, parts, harvest, preparation. These notes are awaiting a citation to a published source. Check them before you rely on them.

Identification

Flat, dark needles, a red fleshy cup around a single seed, and a shrub habit. Cultivated yews are often sheared foundation plants.

Lookalikes

Eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) is a tree with short flat needles and small cones. It is not yew and it is not poison hemlock, and it is not a feed in this guide. If you are looking at foundation-shrub clippings, assume yew until you know otherwise.

Parts to feed

Do not feed needles, twigs, or seeds.

New England timing

Canada yew is a native understory shrub, green whenever it is not buried in snow. The yews that kill animals in New England are often Japanese or English yew planted around houses. All of them count as this entry, all year.

Harvest

Do not dump hedge trimmings into a pasture or a rabbit run.

Preparation

There is no safe amount and no drying step.
